title: The Khaganate That Replaced the Turks
bullets: Around 742 the Uyghurs, Karluks, and Basmyl rose together against the rotting Second Türk Khaganate; by 744 the Uyghur leader Qutlugh Bilge Köl had taken the Orkhon, the steppe's throne room.
In 745 the Uyghurs killed the last Ashina qaghan, Özmiş, and couriered his head to the Tang court — a severed-head announcement that the management of the steppe had changed.
Bayanchur Khan, who took over in 747, built Ordu-Baliq on the Orkhon: a walled, gridded permanent capital, a genuinely strange thing for a nomad empire to build.
By planting a fixed city Bayanchur traded the nomad's classic invulnerability for a tax-and-trade hub — a bet that shaped everything, including how fast it could later be burned.
The Uyghurs cut their own runiform Old Turkic inscriptions, the Shine Usu and Tariat stelae — a thin inside-voice against an otherwise entirely Chinese record.
The state ran on the Toquz Oghuz, the Nine Tribes, with the royal Yaglakar clan at its head, held together only by military success and a cut of the China trade.
744 sat in one of the premodern world's most consequential decades: the Abbasid Revolution came in 750 and the Battle of Talas in 751, the hinge that handed Central Asia's future to Islam.
By 760 a Turkic people who were not the Türks held the Orkhon, ruled from a city, kept written records, and were already the strangest nomad empire the steppe had produced.

title: Creditors of the Tang
bullets: The An Lushan rebellion erupted in December 755 and nearly destroyed Tang China, the wealthiest empire in the world, whose census collapse was so vast historians still argue how much was death versus lost counting.
The cornered Tang court bought Uyghur cavalry; in 757 a combined army retook Luoyang and Chang'an, and the agreed price was that the Uyghurs could sack the recaptured city.
The 762 sack of Luoyang was so severe that the payment citizens made to buy a halt still left tens of thousands dead — a rescue and an extortion at once, as the Chinese sources admit.
The horse-and-silk trade became permanent: the Uyghurs drove broken-winded steppe horses to the frontier and took new silk at a fixed extortionate rate the Tang could not refuse.
Because silk functioned as currency across Inner Asia, the Uyghurs had built a pipeline converting the steppe's surplus into the Silk Road's universal wealth, on a permanent schedule.
In 758 the Tang sent Princess Ningguo, a real imperial daughter, to the Uyghur qaghan — an admission, in the only protocol that mattered, that the steppe was now a power to be courted.
Ningguo refused the Uyghur custom of widow mutilation on the grounds of Tang custom and was eventually allowed home, a rare instance of a woman traded between empires saying no.
For about a decade China did not pay the steppe to stay away; it begged the steppe to come in and then could not afford to make it leave.

title: A Persian Religion on the Steppe
bullets: Default steppe religion was Tengrism, a sky-centered system with no scripture, founder, or church — almost the opposite of what the Uyghurs were about to adopt.
In 762–763, in the wreck of a Luoyang his cavalry was sacking, the qaghan Bögü Khan met Sogdian Manichaean Electi and proclaimed Manichaeism the Uyghur state religion.
Manichaeism was a third-century Persian dualist faith built for export by the prophet Mani; by the 700s it survived mainly along the Silk Road, carried and financed by Sogdian merchants.
It is the only case in history of a steppe empire taking a literate, ascetic, missionary scriptural religion of the settled world as an organ of state.
A scriptural church needs readers: the Uyghurs adapted the Sogdian alphabet into the Old Uyghur script, the direct ancestor of the Mongol and then Manchu writing systems.
The Karabalgasun inscription, a trilingual stele around 808 in Old Turkic, Sogdian, and Chinese, was itself an argument — a state that intended to be read by its elite, its financiers, and China.
The likeliest reasons mix sincerity with structure: binding the court to the Sogdians' faith bound it to their credit networks, and a scriptural ideology unified a sprawling tribal confederation.
The result was the most settled-looking nomad empire yet — urban, literate, mercantile, and dangerously dependent on a single trade, a fixed capital, a foreign diaspora, and a foreign church.

title: Destroyed in a Generation
bullets: Steppe empires usually die slowly; the Uyghur Khaganate died like a settled state whose one city is taken — suddenly, in a single campaigning season.
From the 820s a run of qaghans were enthroned and murdered by their own ministers, burning the legitimacy a tribal confederation cannot easily regrow.
A catastrophic winter at the end of the 830s — a jut, when ice seals the grass and herds starve standing in it — was followed by epidemic and famine the fixed-capital empire could not absorb.
In 840 a disaffected general, Külüg Bagha, guided the Yenisei Kyrgyz onto the heartland; they stormed and burned Ordu-Baliq, killed the qaghan, and ended the khaganate.
The walled capital Bayanchur built to display permanence was the very thing that made the dynasty mortal: it gave the Kyrgyz an address whose burning was the death of the state.
The survivors broke into three migrations — south to the Tang frontier, broken at the Battle of Shahu in 843; west to the Gansu corridor; and southwest into the Tarim oases.
With their Uyghur protectors gone, the Tang crushed Chinese Manichaeism in 842–843, the leading edge of the much larger Huichang persecution of 845.
The Kyrgyz looted the Orkhon and withdrew to Siberia rather than rule it; the steppe's throne then stood empty for 366 years, until Genghis Khan in 1206.

title: From Khaganate to Oasis
bullets: The usual fate of a shattered steppe people is absorption; the Uyghurs instead kept their identity, script, and elite culture by deliberately ceasing to be nomads.
Around 866 a Uyghur leader took the Turfan oases and founded the Kingdom of Qocho, the longest-lived and richest of the oasis Uyghur states, alongside the Ganzhou kingdom in Gansu.

Settling among a Buddhist agrarian population, the Qocho Uyghurs drifted from Manichaeism to Buddhism, with Nestorian Christian and residual Manichaean minorities — royal patronage following popular practice.
Qocho patrons filled the Bezeklik Thousand Buddha Caves with murals fusing Indian, Chinese, Tocharian, and Iranian styles into a distinct Uyghur Buddhist art.
The same literate machinery built for a Persian church produced a vast Old Uyghur Buddhist translation literature, preserved in enormous quantity by the dry Turfan sands.
The oasis Uyghurs became farmers, extending the karez underground-canal system to bloom the Turfan depression, one of the hottest, driest places in Asia.
A Song Chinese envoy, Wang Yande, visited Qocho in 981–984 and described irrigated fields, libraries, and dozens of monasteries — a horse-archer nomad people gone fully agrarian.
By becoming a settled civilization the Uyghurs made themselves a reservoir of literate administrators — exactly what a future conquering nomad would most need and least possess.

title: The First Turkic Muslims
bullets: The Karluks, who took the western steppe in 744, formed the Kara-Khanid Khanate around Kashgar and Balasagun — a pagan Tengrist Turkic power on the Samanid Muslim frontier.
Around 934 the prince Satuq Bughra Khan converted to Islam, seized power, and became the first Turkic Muslim ruler; he later became a saint, his tomb at Artush a pilgrimage site.
Muslim chroniclers report a mass conversion of around 200,000 tents a generation later — a literary figure, but pointing at the real religious tipping point of the steppe.

The Kara-Khanids were the first Turkic Muslim state — not the first Turkic Muslims as persons — which is why the later Ottoman, Mughal, and Anatolian Turkic worlds descend from a tenth-century prince at Kashgar.
In 999 the Kara-Khanids took Bukhara and ended the Persian Samanid dynasty, putting Transoxiana under Turkic Muslim rule for the first time in history.
Around 1069 Yusuf Khass Hajib's Kutadgu Bilig became the first major literary work of Islamic Turkic civilization — a steppe language sitting down as an author, not a subject.
Mahmud al-Kashgari's Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk of 1072–1074, a vast Turkic-Arabic dictionary with the earliest Turkic-centered world map, argued the Islamic world needed to understand the Turks.
By 1089 the Seljuks had forced the western Kara-Khanids into vassalage — the first Turkic Muslim dynasty already being absorbed into the larger order it helped inaugurate.

title: The Buddhists Who Ruled the Muslims
bullets: In 1125 the Jurchen destroyed the Khitan Liao empire; a Liao prince, Yelü Dashi, led a few thousand followers two thousand miles west.
Yelü Dashi held the jinshi, the highest Chinese civil-service degree, and carried west not just a war-band but the idea of a Chinese-style centralized state.
Around 1132 he proclaimed himself Gurkhan and founded the Qara-Khitai, the Western Liao — a Buddhist, Chinese-institutioned dynasty on Muslim soil.
At the Battle of Qatwan near Samarkand in 1141 he annihilated the Great Seljuk sultan Sanjar — the largest defeat of a Muslim army in Central Asia to that point.
The Qara-Khitai ruled a majority-Muslim Central Asia by indirect rule and light, famously moderate taxation, leaving vassals their religion and law and converting no one.
Distorted news of Qatwan reached Crusader Europe as the rumor of a great Christian king beyond Islam — one of the documented roots of the Prester John legend.
Muslim sources themselves, chiefly the Persian official Juvayni, remembered the era as stable, prosperous, and just — a faint surprise that is part of the evidence.
Ruling by a light touch over proud intact vassals works only while the center can still win; by the 1190s the system was one hard shock from coming apart.

title: The Eve of the Mongols
bullets: On the steppe the Uyghurs had abandoned in 840, a Mongol war-leader spent two decades destroying his rivals; in 1206 an assembly on the Onon River proclaimed him Genghis Khan.
The Orkhon, empty for 366 years, had an emperor again — the interregnum this book occupies is exactly the gap between the last Orkhon empire and the next.
The Buddhist Uyghur idiqut of Qocho, Barchuq, submitted voluntarily in 1209, killing the Qara-Khitai resident before he was attacked, and was rewarded as a fifth son of Genghis Khan.
Küchlüg, a fugitive Naiman prince, usurped the Qara-Khitai throne around 1211 and then persecuted its Muslim majority — destroying the dynasty's defining tolerance just before the Mongols arrived.
In 1218 the Mongol general Jebe took the realm by proclaiming religious freedom, restoring exactly the tolerance Küchlüg had wrecked, then hunted Küchlüg down and killed him.
The Mongols adopted the Old Uyghur alphabet for their own language; the captured Uyghur scribe Tatatonga taught the Mongol princes writing and the use of the state seal.
The Qocho Uyghurs became the Mongol Empire's tutors, tax administrators, and chancery clerks, and the oasis ortoq partnerships became the empire-wide Mongol ortogh system.
The Mongols supplied the cavalry and the terror; the world this book describes supplied the alphabet, the clerks, the accountants, and the operating manual.
